entities.summary:
Gaspar de Ávalos de la Cueva (1485–1545), also known as Gaspar Dávalos de la Cueva, was a prominent Spanish Roman Catholic bishop and cardinal whose ecclesiastical career spanned a pivotal era of consolidation for the Spanish Empire and the Catholic Church. Rising from noble Castilian lineage, his influence was primarily felt within the Iberian Peninsula, where he served as Archbishop of Santiago de Compostela and, most notably, as Archbishop of Seville. His tenure coincided with the initial phases of the Catholic Reformation and the expansion of Spanish power, positioning him as a key figure in the spiritual and administrative governance of one of Europe's most powerful realms.

Ávalos de la Cueva's career was marked by a series of significant appointments, reflecting his standing within both the Church and the Spanish monarchy. He was appointed Archbishop of Santiago de Compostela in 1524, a major pilgrimage site, before being transferred to the influential Archdiocese of Seville in 1539. Seville, as the gateway to the Americas, was a crucial administrative and economic hub, and Ávalos de la Cueva played a vital role in managing its vast ecclesiastical affairs. Pope Paul III elevated him to cardinal in 1544, assigning him the title of Cardinal-Priest of San Marcello al Corso. His administrative acumen and commitment to ecclesiastical discipline were highly valued by Emperor Charles V, who relied on such figures to reinforce religious orthodoxy and imperial authority across his domains.

Gaspar de Ávalos de la Cueva (1485–1545), also named Gaspar Dávalos de la Cueva, was a Spanish Roman Catholic bishop and cardinal. He played a pivotal role in the Counter-Reformation within the Catholic Church.

As Bishop of Málaga from 1527 until his death, he implemented numerous reforms aimed at strengthening the Catholic faith among the population.

De la Cueva's tenure saw the establishment of the Congregation for the Evangelical Schools, which focused on promoting Catholic education in Spain. He also contributed to the compilation of the Index Librorum Prohibitorum (Index of Prohibited Books), a list of books deemed heretical or objectionable by the Church.

De la Cueva's legacy extends beyond his administrative reforms; he was also an influential figure in the theological debates surrounding the Eucharistic theology and the sacraments. His writings on these subjects continue to be studied by scholars today.

In a broader sense, de la Cueva's efforts during this period reflect the complex web of religious, political, and social forces that shaped the late medieval landscape. This era was marked by widespread religious strife, as the Protestant Reformation challenged traditional Catholic teachings and practices.
